title: Go to each side (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 12)
hook: Aaron went to each side of a quarrel, telling each how sorry the other was
tomorrow: how small can a first step be and still count?

segments.voice: Yesterday, God left one wounding phrase out of Sarah's words, and Hillel and Shammai argued over praising a bride. Great is peace. Today, someone who made peace with his feet.

Two friends at the same lunch table, eating with their shoulders turned half away from each other. Everybody feels it; nobody says it. You can almost hear the silence between them. Then lunch ends, and they leave by different doors. Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an old companion to the sayings of the sages, tells how Aaron, the brother of Moses, handled exactly this, and the answer to yesterday's question starts with where he sat down.
screen: `SHOULDERS TURNED AWAY.` → `A SILENCE YOU CAN HEAR.` → `WHERE AARON SAT DOWN.`

segments.voice: When two people quarreled, Aaron went and sat down beside one of them. Sat: not a summons, not a lecture. And he said, my son, look at what your friend is going through. He's tearing at his heart, ripping his clothes, saying: how can I lift my eyes and face my friend? I'm ashamed. I'm the one who wronged him. Aaron stayed beside him until the anger left his heart. Then he went and sat beside the other one, and said the same. And when the two met, they embraced and kissed. The high priest of Israel, in this picture, spends his days on this: one quarrel at a time, one person at a time. The midrash ties it to Aaron's death: the Torah says all the house of Israel wept for him. Now notice the senses in it. Sitting beside, not across. Torn clothes. A hug at the end. Peace here is something a body does: Aaron walks to one side, then walks to the other. The midrash doesn't say whether the friend had already said those words out loud; some readers hear yesterday's lesson in it, great is peace. Here's the line to repeat tonight: in the Mishnah, Hillel says be among the students of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing it, rodef shalom. Pursuing. You can't do that sitting still.
screen: `HE SAT DOWN BESIDE ONE.` · `THEN BESIDE THE OTHER.` · `THEY MET, AND EMBRACED.` · `RODEF SHALOM: PURSUE IT.` · then, large: `GO TO EACH SIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit with an empty space beside you, and turn your shoulders a little toward it, the way Aaron sat next to each person rather than across from them. Picture someone in a quarrel right now sitting there, and stay with them without fixing anything. Halfway through, turn the other way and sit beside the other side.
screen: `AN EMPTY SPACE BESIDE YOU.` · `BESIDE, NOT ACROSS.` · `THEN TURN TO THE OTHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: Go to each side: Aaron's way of making peace in Avot de-Rabbi Natan. Sit with one, then with the other, until the two can meet.
Keep this one: go to each side. Aaron didn't send a message across the room; he walked over and sat down.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching holds up Aaron as the model peacemaker: Hillel's saying in Pirkei Avot, 'be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace', is often taught with this story, and making peace between people (shalom bayit, hava'at shalom) is counted as a mitzvah.

notes: Avot de-Rabbi Natan A 12 paraphrased (Aaron sits with one, describes the other tearing his heart and garments in shame, stays until the jealousy/anger leaves; then the other; they embrace and kiss when they meet; hence Numbers 20:29 'all the house of Israel'). Confirm details and chapter.
